Après l’attentat de la mosquée de Québec: After the Quebec City mosque attack, the Muslim community is strengthening its unity to make its voice heard.

L’idée de cet article est née presque ma: The idea for this article came almost in spite of myself, as I noticed a subtle shift during the January 29 commemorations: beyond quiet reflection, something had more to do with organizing and looking ahead than with the duty of remembrance alone. It was less the official speeches than the conversations on the sidelines, the panels and certain personal announcements (notably Aymen Derbali’s) that made me want to explore the question: what comes after remembrance?
Le travail s’est fait sur place, à Québe: The work was done on the ground in Quebec City, over the course of the activities surrounding the commemoration. The mood was not marked by the mistrust I had sometimes felt while preparing other stories, but rather by a kind of lucid weariness: many of the people I spoke with talked willingly, while pointing out that they felt they had been repeating the same observations for years.
Parmi les découvertes marquantes, il y a: Among the most striking discoveries was the contrast between the very real diversity of backgrounds and a shared concern: how to turn a demographic and social presence into visible collective capacity for action, without erasing internal differences?
This article does not aim to be exhaustive. Rather, it seeks to capture a turning point as it presented itself to be seen and heard: a space where remembrance remains central, but where the idea of organizing and ordinary citizenship is beginning to take up as much room as the memory itself.
<strong>Le silence dure quelques seconde: The silence lasts a few seconds longer than expected in the room, as if the audience hesitated to applaud. On January 29, 2026, at the commemoration evening organized by the City of Quebec in memory of the victims of the 2017 attack, Aymen Derbali speaks before nearly 150 people. A survivor of the tragedy, hit by seven bullets fired from the terrorist’s Glock pistol, Aymen publicly announces for the first time his formal involvement in organizing the commemorations and his intention to step up his commitment to defending the rights of Muslims. “The duty of remembrance is also to fight the cause of the tragedy,” he tells La Converse, drawing a parallel between the fight against Islamophobia and the commitment that losing a loved one to an illness inspires. In the room, many nod in agreement. This year, beyond quiet reflection, another word runs through the speeches: unity. Around the chairs still lined up, the Sainte-Foy district council chamber is already buzzing with overlapping conversations. Officials, victims’ families, members of the Muslim community and longtime friends chat in a surprisingly light atmosphere, made up of lingering handshakes, shy smiles and restrained embraces. Solemnity gradually gives way to a kind of shared warmth. Report
Neuf ans après l’attentat qui a coûté la: Nine years after the attack that took the lives of six worshippers at the Quebec City mosque, the commemoration remains an emotionally charged moment. But for some, it is also a tipping point. “This year, what’s different is that I’m now a member of the organizing committee,” Aymen Derbali says in an interview. Around him, other wounded survivors are getting involved, he says, naming Nizar Ghali and Saïd Akjour in particular. “We need to open up even more, make even more effort to get the real message across.”
Au Québec depuis 2001, M. Derbali a insi: In Quebec since 2001, Mr. Derbali stressed the profile of the victims in his address: “Fathers, good workers, people active in society who chose Quebec to build their families.”
S’il désigne explicitement l’islamophobi: While he explicitly names Islamophobia as the driving force behind the tragedy, he also insists on what he describes as a persistent lack of understanding of Islam in the public sphere. For him, engagement follows a simple logic: “When someone dies of an illness, you get involved with a foundation to fight that illness. Here, the cause is Islamophobia.”
Le lendemain, un documentaire projeté da: The next day, a documentary screened as part of the commemoration activities revives memories that are still raw. On the screen, the faces of survivors and victims’ loved ones follow one another, between accounts of irreversible loss and testimonies of an outpouring of solidarity from across Quebec society after the attack. In the room, several viewers discreetly wipe away tears, while others nod as some speakers express their frustration with measures deemed insufficient to prevent Islamophobic acts.
L’appel à l’engagement individuel trouve: The call for individual engagement finds a broader echo within the community, notably among its leaders, such as Boufeldja Bouabdallah, co-founder of the Grande Mosquée de Québec.
Nous le rencontrons dans un café-restaur: We meet him at a café-restaurant right across from the Grande Mosquée de Québec, a place he visits regularly. He is finishing a steaming bowl of soup when we arrive, wipes his hands, smiles broadly and almost apologizes for making us wait a few seconds. The conversation begins informally, between two greetings to regulars passing by the table. For Mr. Bouabdallah, the need for unity goes beyond symbolism. It is about the collective ability to be heard. “We’ve never presented a single face,” he says, pointing to scattered positions and petitions launched separately.
Pourtant, au fil des années, <l1>le poid: Yet over the years, <l1>the demographic weight of the Muslim population has grown. </l1>According to 2021 census data, it makes up 4.9% of the Canadian population, or nearly 1.8 million people, nearly a third of whom were born in the country. In Quebec, that proportion reaches 5.1%, or more than 420,000 people.
C’est aussi durant ces années de croissa: It was also during these years of growth that Quebec’s Muslim community felt targeted by a series of laws deemed to infringe on its rights and freedoms. The resurgence community leaders are showing today stems from a need to shake off this position as the weak link.
Pour Boufeldja Bouabdallah, l’appel à l’: For Boufeldja Bouabdallah, the call for unity first responds to an accumulated sense of powerlessness over recent legislative debates, notably the secularism law. And those said to strengthen secularism. In his view, the lack of coordination prevented the community from truly influencing certain political decisions. “We couldn’t change the course of certain articles because we weren’t united,” he says, citing scattered petitions and interventions carried out “each on their own.” In a system where “it also works with the masses,” he continues, the stakes are not merely symbolic: “When sixty thousand people speak with one voice, you can’t brush them aside.” Unity thus becomes, in his eyes, a condition for “showing that we are capable people” and having a recognized interlocutor with the authorities.
Selon lui, l’enjeu n’est pas seulement r: In his view, the issue is not only religious but also organizational and civic. He speaks of underused skills (lawyers, executives, graduates) and of a fear of state authority inherited from countries of origin. “We’re always afraid of the State, as if it had a stick. But here, the State obeys laws.” Refusing to speak bluntly of political immaturity, he instead describes “a legacy” that is gradually fading. “Before, we said nothing. Now, people speak up. There’s progress.”
Cette lecture de la situation trouve un: This reading of the situation finds strong resonance with Samira Laouni, co-founder of <l1>Muslim Awareness Week</l1>, who traces the origin of the fragmentation well before the recent debates. Having arrived in Quebec in the late 1990s, she says she noticed internal divisions very early on, even though the Muslim presence was numerically smaller. “The Sunni-Shia divide was glaring, and even among Sunnis, it existed between schools of jurisprudence, then between nationalities: Moroccans, Algerians…”
Pour elle, cette fragmentation relève d’: For her, this fragmentation stems from long-standing conditioning. “We grew up with the ‘where are you from.’ It’s a division that was instilled in us, inherited in part from colonization.” She believes the political tensions of the countries of origin continue to be imported into Quebec “as if we were going to settle here the problems of over there”; a logic she considers counterproductive for people who left those contexts precisely to get away from them.
Au-delà des clivages identitaires, Samir: Beyond identity-based divisions, Samira Laouni also speaks of organizational mechanisms. She describes a “competition to carve out a place” among organizations and community leaders, which she says she experienced from the inside during the mobilization against the Charter of Values from 2011 to 2013. “Every time, it was: who’s going to speak, which organization will be out front, when we were all gathered under the same umbrella!” In addition, she says, there are patriarchal dynamics and a lack of shared governance culture (respecting speaking turns, listening, meeting methods), which she calls the “ABCs” of collective functioning. Self-criticism is therefore necessary, she says, to move beyond institutional ego and learn to work together.
Elle insiste également sur l’importance: She also stresses the importance of local civic and political participation, arguing that visibility should not be limited to moments of crisis or commemoration.
<strong>Une diversité de voix, une même: A diversity of voices, a shared concern
Pour Boufeldja Bouabdallah comme pour Sa: For Boufeldja Bouabdallah as for Samira Laouni, unity does not mean cultural or religious uniformity, but the ability to move beyond origin-based affiliations and rivalries between organizations in order to act under one banner when the issues affect the whole community. One stresses the weight of numbers and active citizenship, the other introspection and working methods. Two converging diagnoses that describe less a lack of will than a persistent difficulty in turning internal diversity into visible collective strength.
Dans un article précédent, consacré à la: In a previous article on <l1>the security of Quebec City mosques, nine years after the attack</l1>, several people interviewed by La Converse pointed to a rise in Islamophobic attacks and micro-aggressions, both in public spaces and on social media.
Lors d’un panel organisé dans le cadre d: At a panel organized as part of the commemorations, on the theme “Unity in Action,” Eduardo Alves Dos Anjos, a Brazilian convert to Islam, suggested that the treatment of minorities is “a thermometer of society,” arguing for an approach based on dialogue and mutual recognition.
Autre panéliste et survivant de l’attent: Another panellist and survivor of the attack, Mohamed El Hafid, approached the question from the angle of cognitive biases and mechanisms of polarization, stressing the influence of public discourse and socioeconomic inequalities in shaping perceptions. Aware of the stakes, both stressed the need to combine “internal unity” and “external openness.”
Dans la salle, la diversité du public fr: In the room, the diversity of the audience is almost as striking as that of the speakers. Veiled women sit alongside others who are not, familiar faces from the community chat with neighbours who came “simply to be there.” Among them, a woman pastor takes part in the discussions. This plural presence gives the exchanges a tone that is less defensive than dialogical. The word love comes up often.
<strong>L’union par le concret : la Tabl: Unity in practice: the Table de concertation
Au-delà des mots, cette volonté d’unité: Beyond words, this desire for unity is taking the form of structures. The Table de concertation des organisations musulmanes du Québec (TCOM), which brings together about fifteen mosques and organizations, plays a central role in this kind of dynamic. Created in the early 2010s, it recently announced that it is beginning a new chapter in its evolution, aimed at gaining official legal recognition.
Dans un communiqué publié en janvier, la: In a press release published in January, the TCOM speaks of an “engagement resolutely focused on action,” with the adoption of a mission, a vision and a roadmap built around three pillars: governance, internal cohesion and external impact. The stated goal? To strengthen cohesion among its members and ensure “a structured, legitimate and constructive presence in the public sphere.”
Intervenant au nom de la TCOM lors du pa: Speaking on behalf of the TCOM at the panel mentioned above, Souheil Hassine described the organization as a space of cohesion among about fifteen mosques in different regions, including Quebec City, Rimouski and Rivière-du-Loup. The TCOM helped “manage the crisis that followed the attack” and the pandemic, while speaking “with one voice” to authorities and the media, he noted. The TCOM has also taken part in writing briefs submitted during legislative debates, illustrating its desire to work within existing institutional mechanisms.
<strong>Désir de citoyenneté ordinaire,: A desire for ordinary citizenship, the fragility of recognition
Retour à la commémoration officielle au: Back at the official commemoration at the Sainte-Foy council headquarters. That evening, Aymen Derbali stayed until the last guests left, talking with everyone despite visible fatigue. Quadriplegic as a result of the bullets he took in 2017, he responds to requests with patience and a constant smile. He smiles easily and has an affable presence, showing a kind of quiet resilience that goes beyond his own personal story.
Entre les notes universelles d’un trio à: Between the universal notes of an all-women string trio, his commitment sketches the idea of a memory that is no longer limited to remembrance, but now seeks concrete forms of action.
C’est précisément cette articulation ent: It is precisely this link between lived experience and public recognition that is shaken a few days later. On February 4, as we finish this article, the Canadian government announces the abolition of the position of Special Representative on Combatting Islamophobia, <l1>created by Justin Trudeau’s government in January 2023 and held by Amira Elghawaby</l1>. For many community stakeholders, the very existence of this role was an institutional signal, if not a sufficient response, then at least a formal recognition of a phenomenon that many feel is still under-named in the political sphere.
Entre la volonté d’organisation exprimée: Between the desire to organize expressed during the commemorations, the calls for unity and the disappearance of a federal role dedicated to this fight, one thread remains: that of an ordinary citizenship that many say they want to exercise fully, while noting that institutional recognition of the realities they name remains fragile.
